title: Prompt canonicalization refactor — personal plan and notes
content:
Context:
This is my working notes for a small project: reduce duplicate/near-duplicate prompts in our internal prompt library and create a lightweight canonicalization flow that is reversible and audit-friendly. Goal is to make searching, evaluation and rollout easier (and cheaper) without losing human-intent fidelity.

Why now:
- Library has grown organically; many templates differ only by wording or placeholder order.
- Regression alerts (quality drift) get noisy because multiple near-identical prompts each get separate tracking.
- Small engineering effort could cut eval surface area and improve rerun speed for A/B tests.

Constraints / non-goals:
- Not a full rewrite of semantic intent; we should not merge prompts across distinct intents.
- Keep change traceable: every canonicalization step must be reversible and annotated.
- Avoid heavy compute (no exhaustive pairwise embeddings across 10k prompts today).

High-level approach (incremental):
1) Define canonical schema for a prompt artifact (PromCan v0):
   - id: stable id (existing library id if present)
   - canonical_text: normalized template string (placeholders canonicalized)
   - placeholders: ordered list of placeholder names (strings)
   - intent_tags: small set of labels (customer-facing, summarize, safety-filter, etc.)
   - example_inputs: 1-3 representative inputs
   - provenance: original_ids (list) + canonicalization_notes
   - hashes: (sha1 of canonical_text) and short fingerprint (first8)

2) Lightweight normalization rules (apply in order):
   a) Unicode normalize (NFC) and trim whitespace
   b) Lowercase except for preserved-role tokens (like PERSON_NAME placeholders)
   c) Collapse repeated punctuation ("!!!" -> "!")
   d) Normalize numeric tokens to <NUM> unless context demands otherwise
   e) Replace recognized placeholders with canonical markers: {user}, {topic}, {examples}, {format}
   f) Sort non-positional metadata tuples (e.g., tags)

3) Merge heuristics (do not auto-merge — mark candidates):
   - Lexical edit distance on normalized text < 12 and shared placeholder schema -> candidate
   - Embedding cosine similarity > 0.94 (sparse candidate set only) -> candidate
   - Intent-tag overlap >= 0.7 -> candidate score +0.15
   - If candidate score >= 0.8, flag for manual review

4) Manual review workflow (ui + checklist):
   - Show original texts side-by-side with diffs highlighting placeholder changes
   - Show 3 auto-generated outputs for both prompts on a small eval suite
   - Checklist items: intent match? contextual edgecases? expected token delta? privacy tags OK?

Examples (toy):
Original A: "Summarize the following article in 3 bullets:
{article_text}
Be concise."
Original B: "Give me a short 3-bullet summary of this article:
{article_text}
Keep it concise."

After normalization -> canonical_text: "summarize article in 3 bullets: {article_text} — be concise"
placeholders -> ["article_text"]
Note: canonical hash: sha1("summarize article in 3 bullets: {article_text} — be concise") -> 3f2a7b0c

Edgecase: positional templates where order changes meaning: e.g.,
  "Rewrite {input} for {audience}." vs "Rewrite for {audience}: {input}."
These should preserve placeholder order and be considered non-identical unless reviewer approves merging.

Failure modes to watch (from quick experiments):
- Over-normalization: canonicalizing numbers or capitalizations that encode meaning ("COVID-19" -> "covid-<NUM>" loses signal)
- Placeholder mismatch: two prompts that look similar but use placeholders with different semantics ("{resume_text}" vs "{job_description}")
- Eval blindness: merged prompts mask subtle quality differences when using small eval sets

Small eval harness (local):
- Script: tools/eval/can_compare.sh --pair <idA> <idB> --suite smoke10
- Metrics: semantic-similarity (embedding), ROUGE, response-length, instruction-following score (heuristic)
- Quick rule: if instruction-following differs > 0.12 on mean, treat as not-equivalent

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (1 week): run canonicalizer on a 2k prompt sample, generate candidate merge list, collect notes
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): manual review of top-50 merges with team (Maya + Ravi), tag approves -> create canonical artifacts but keep original ids in provenance
- Phase 2 (4 weeks): wire canonical artifacts into internal search and eval dashboards (read-only first)
- Phase 3: optional redirect of ingestion -> prefer canonicalized variant for new entries; keep original text as alt_text

Operational details / small UX notes:
- Add a small flag in the search UI: "Show canonicalized variants" (on by default for internal users)
- Keep a human-readable canonicalization log per artifact: plain text note explaining why merge happened
- Add a "revert" button that restores original mapping and tags the canonical artifact with reverted_by and reason

Open questions / TODOs:
- Which embeddings model to use for similarity? ada-embed-002 is cheap but noisy; consider higher-tier for candidate scoring (costs vs. accuracy).
- Threshold tuning: should we do a small gridsearch using a labeled set of 200 manual pair judgments? (yes)
- How to handle prompts that deliberately abuse punctuation/emoji as a style signal? Probably preserve special chars in a style field.
- Want to prototype a PromCan CLI that outputs a side-by-side markdown report for reviewers.

Short-term next actions (this week):
- Run normalization pipeline on 2k sample and produce top-200 candidate merges (Elliot).
- Create a tiny labeling form (Google Form or linear ticket template) for manual judgments (Maya).
- Draft RFC for the canonical schema (Ravi + me) and link to PR.

Notes to self:
- Keep canonical_text human-readable; don't try to compress into tokens-only form.
- Always store original text; provenance is critical when customers ask why variant changed.
- Keep performance benefit estimates conservative: expect 8–15% reduction in eval runs initially, more as we prune.

Snippets (prompts to test the harness):
- "Summarize the article in 3 concise bullets: {article_text}."
- "Create a short list of 3 bullets summarizing the passage: {article_text}."
- "Rewrite the following for a nontechnical manager: {input_text}."
- "Paraphrase for a manager: {input_text}."

If you read this later: TODO log decisions inline and tag artifacts with "promcan-v0" so we can filter experiments easily.

End of notes.
